title: Olivetti Launches the Programma 101, Forerunner of the Personal Computer
reason: Multiple independent sources corroborate every material element. IEEE Spectrum (a reputable technical publication) confirms the Programma 101 was "Introduced at a Business Equipment Manufacturers Association [BEMA] show in New York in October 1965," designed by Pier Giorgio Perotto, and that "about 10 Programma 101 were sold to NASA and used to plan the Apollo 11 landing on the Moon." Italian government cultural site opportunitaly.gov.it independently confirms the exact date "15 October 1965 at the BEMA Show in New York" and that "some 44,000 units were sold" between 1965 and 1971, mostly in the US (a figure echoed by finestresullarte.info and other design-history outlets, some of which round to ~40,000 in Olivetti's own later summary — within the "roughly 44,000" stated). The "forerunner of the personal computer" characterization is widely repeated across historical/design sources (Inexhibit, finestresullarte.info, Adriano Olivetti Foundation). The Apple I influence claim is also a commonly repeated claim in secondary tech-history commentary (e.g., Pingdom's history piece), though it is looser/more anecdotal than the other facts and not confirmed by the most authoritative sources (IEEE Spectrum, Wikipedia) — it is a minor supplementary claim, not the load-bearing part of the description, and its inclusion does not contradict any verified fact. Core facts (actor, product, designer, date, location, unit sales magnitude, NASA/Apollo 11 use, historical significance) all check out as described.

verifications.reason: Multiple independent sources confirm the core facts: Olivetti's Programma 101, designed by Pier Giorgio Perotto (with industrial design by Mario Bellini), was formally introduced at the BEMA (Business Equipment Manufacturers Association) trade show in New York on 15 October 1965. IEEE Spectrum, Wikipedia, and Italy's official trade promotion site (opportunitaly.gov.it) all corroborate this date/venue and Perotto's role. Sales figures of approximately 44,000 units (sources range 40,000-44,000, with ~90% in the US) sold through 1971 are confirmed by multiple sources. NASA's use of P101 units (about 10 purchased) for Apollo 11 mission calculations (trajectories, lunar module antenna positioning) is corroborated by both Wikipedia and IEEE Spectrum. It is widely described across sources as the forerunner/first personal computer. The one detail I could not independently corroborate is the specific claim that it "influenced Apple's design of the Apple I" -- English Wikipedia's Programma 101 article makes no mention of Apple, and I found no independent source directly linking it to the Apple I's design (the well-documented Olivetti IP dispute from this era was with Hewlett-Packard's 9100A, not Apple). This is a secondary/embellished detail that does not affect the year, country, or the core magnitude/actor/scope of the event, so it does not change the verdict to PARTIAL.
